One: what Ibn Abbas related, that Abraha ibn al-Sabbah built a white church called al-Qulays, and wrote to the Negus: "I will not stop until I divert the pilgrimage of the Arabs to it." Concerning this, Ikrimah ibn Amir ibn Hashim ibn Abd Manaf says:

"O God, disgrace al-Aswad ibn Maqsud,
who seized the herd, in which were garlands,
held between Hira and Thabir and the wilderness,
and gathered them with the dark-spotted ones, dragged away,
they agreed that there should be no worshipped one,
and that they would demolish the sacred ancient House,
and al-Marwatayn and the dark sacred sites.
O Lord, protect it, for You are praised."

Abd al-Muttalib, who was handsome, tall, and whom the eye could not take hold of, went to Abraha and asked him about his camels that had been taken. Abraha said: "I was impressed by you when I saw you, but now I have lost interest in you." He said: "Why?" so defend Your sanctuary.

then it is a matter that is manifest to You."

Abd al-Muttalib went out, headed to Abraha and asked him about his camels, and he returned them mockingly, so that he would return to seize them when he entered Mecca.

Scholars differed about whether the Negus was with them or not. Some said he was with them, while others said he was not with them.

The army headed to Mecca to burn the Kaaba. When Abd al-Muttalib turned away with his camels, he took refuge with them in the mountains of Mecca, and headed to Mecca by the way of Mina. The elephant, when it was sent toward the Sanctuary, would balk, and when it was turned away from it, it would advance. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said the name of the elephant was Mahmud. Aisha said: "I saw the elephant's driver and its leader, both blind and paralysed, begging food from the people of Mecca."

They halted at al-Mughammas, and Abdullah ibn Makhzum said:

"You are the Majestic, our Lord, unstained,
You held back the elephant at al-Mughammas,
You held it in the state of the overturned,
and for them there is no escape nor respite."

Al-Mukarkas means: thrown down and overturned.(p-341)

The people of Mecca saw birds approaching from the direction of the sea. Abd al-Muttalib said: "These are strange birds in our land; they are neither Najdi, nor Tihami, nor Hijazi; they are like the yaʿasib (locusts/swarms), and in their beaks and feet were stones. Ata ibn Abi Rabah said: "The birds came in the evening and went away, then they came upon them at dawn and struck them." Ata al-Awfi said: "I asked Abu Said al-Khudri about them, and he said: 'They are the pigeons of Mecca.'"

Abraha escaped from the people and returned to Yemen, but he perished on the way.

Al-Waqidi said: Abraha was the grandfather of the Negus who was in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ. When they were certain of the destruction of the people, the poet said:

"Where is the escape, and the God is the seeker,
the cut-nosed defeated one, is not the victor."

By "the cut-nosed one" he means Abraha; he was so called because Aryat struck him with a spear and split his nose and forehead, that is, some of it fell upon the other.

none disputes them except the ungrateful.
He held back the elephant at al-Mughammas until
it passed, howling as if it were gored."

"O Lord, we do not hope for anything from them except You.
O Lord, protect Your sanctuary from them.
Indeed the enemy of the House is one who opposes You.
Protect them from destroying Your sanctuary."

When his father saw this, he said: "My son is the most horsemanship-skilled of the Arabs, and he would not uncover his thigh except as a bearer of good news or a warner."

When he drew near their assembly, close enough to make them hear, they said: "What is behind you?" He said: "They have all perished." "You prevented the Abyssinians and the elephants,

and every affair of theirs was a confounded affair (ma'dal)."

One: that their plot led them astray until they perished.

The second: that their destruction led their plot astray until it was nullified.

"Indeed Salul, may death overtake you, is a gratitude,

meaning: scattered.

The fourth: that ababil means of differing colours, said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The fifth: that it means a group after a group, said by Abu Salih and Ata, and from it is the poet's saying:

"And ababil of horses upon them,

"And a host striking the helmets from the side,

O Lord, protect it, for You are praised."

Abd al-Muttalib, who was handsome, tall, and whom the eye could not take hold of, went to Abraha and asked him about his camels that had been taken. Abraha said: "I was impressed by you when I saw you, but now I have lost interest in you." He said: "Why?" He replied: "I came to demolish a house which is your religion and the religion of your forefathers, and you did not speak to me about it, but you spoke to me about your two hundred camels." Abd al-Muttalib said: "I am the owner of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it." Abraha said: "He will not be able to protect it from me." Abd al-Muttalib said: "Tubba', Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan and Khosrow sought it, but they were unable to prevail over it, and you are (like) them." So Abraha returned his camels to him. Abd al-Muttalib went out and returned to Mecca, informed the Quraysh of taking refuge in the mountains, came to the House, took hold of the ring of the door and began saying:

"O God, indeed a servant defends his riding-beast,
so defend Your sanctuary.
Let not their cross and their might prevail over Your might
tomorrow.
If You are leaving them and Your qibla,
then it is a matter that is manifest to You."

Al-Mihal means: strength.(p-340)

Two: what al-Kalbi and Muqatil related (one of them adding and the other reducing) is that a group of youths from Quraysh went out to the land of Abyssinia as merchants, and they alighted on the seashore at a church of the Christians, in a sand dune of it. Al-Kalbi said the church is called Masirjiyan, and Muqatil said it is called al-Haykal. They lit a fire for their food and left it and departed; a violent wind blew, the church caught fire and burned. A messenger came to the Negus and informed him, and he flared up in anger. Abraha ibn al-Sabbah, Hajar ibn Sharahbil and Abu Yaksum al-Kindiyyun came to him and guaranteed to him the burning of the Kaaba and the capture of Mecca. The Negus was the king, Abraha was the commander of the army, Abu Yaksum was the king's boon-companion, and it was said his vizier, and Hajar ibn Sharahbil was one of his commanders. Mujahid said Abu Yaksum was Abraha ibn al-Sabbah. They marched with the army, and with them the elephant. Most said it was a single elephant, while al-Dahhak said there were eight elephants. They alighted at Dhu al-Majaz and seized the herd of Mecca, which included the camels of Abd al-Muttalib. A herdsman came as a warner, climbed al-Safa and shouted: "Wa-sabahah!" Then he informed the people of the coming of the army and the elephant. Abd al-Muttalib went out, headed to Abraha and asked him about his camels, and he returned them mockingly, so that he would return to seize them when he entered Mecca.

Scholars differed about whether the Negus was with them or not. Some said he was with them, while others said he was not with them.

The army headed to Mecca to burn the Kaaba. When Abd al-Muttalib turned away with his camels, he took refuge with them in the mountains of Mecca, and headed to Mecca by the way of Mina. The elephant, when it was sent toward the Sanctuary, would balk, and when it was turned away from it, it would advance. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said the name of the elephant was Mahmud. Aisha said: "I saw the elephant's driver and its leader, both blind and paralysed, begging food from the people of Mecca."

They halted at al-Mughammas, and Abdullah ibn Makhzum said:

"You are the Majestic, our Lord, unstained,
You held back the elephant at al-Mughammas,
You held it in the state of the overturned,
and for them there is no escape nor respite."

Al-Mukarkas means: thrown down and overturned.(p-341)

The people of Mecca saw birds approaching from the direction of the sea. Abd al-Muttalib said: "These are strange birds in our land; they are neither Najdi, nor Tihami, nor Hijazi; they are like the yaʿasib (locusts/swarms), and in their beaks and feet were stones. When they came over the people, they dropped them upon them until they perished." Ata ibn Abi Rabah said: "The birds came in the evening and went away, then they came upon them at dawn and struck them." Ata al-Awfi said: "I asked Abu Said al-Khudri about them, and he said: 'They are the pigeons of Mecca.'"

Abraha escaped from the people and returned to Yemen, but he perished on the way.

Al-Waqidi said: Abraha was the grandfather of the Negus who was in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ. When they were certain of the destruction of the people, the poet said:

"Where is the escape, and the God is the seeker,
the cut-nosed defeated one, is not the victor."

By "the cut-nosed one" he means Abraha; he was so called because Aryat struck him with a spear and split his nose and forehead, that is, some of it fell upon the other.

Abu al-Salt ibn Masud said, and it is said that Abd al-Muttalib said it:

"Indeed the signs of our Lord are clear,
none disputes them except the ungrateful.
He held back the elephant at al-Mughammas until
it passed, howling as if it were gored."

His saying: ﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾ Because they intended the plot of the Quraysh by killing and capturing, and the plot against the House by destruction and demolition.

It is related from Abd al-Muttalib, after what we have related from him, that he took hold of the ring of the door and said:

"O Lord, we do not hope for anything from them except You.
O Lord, protect Your sanctuary from them.
Indeed the enemy of the House is one who opposes You.
Protect them from destroying Your sanctuary."

Then Abd al-Muttalib sent his son Abdullah on a swift horse of his, to see what they had met; he found the people crushed, so he returned galloping, uncovering his thigh. When his father saw this, he said: "My son is the most horsemanship-skilled of the Arabs, and he would not uncover his thigh except as a bearer of good news or a warner."

When he drew near their assembly, close enough to make them hear, they said: "What is behind you?" He said: "They have all perished." Abd al-Muttalib and his companions went out and took their wealth, which became the wealth of the sons of Abd al-Muttalib, and by it Abd al-Muttalib's leadership was established, because he carried away whatever he wished of gold and silver. Then the people of Mecca went out after him and plundered. Abd al-Muttalib said:

"You prevented the Abyssinians and the elephants,
and they had grazed in Mecca the pastures,
and we feared from them fighting,
and every affair of theirs was a confounded affair (ma'dal)."

"And thanks and praise to You, O Possessor of Majesty."

The going astray of their plot may bear two interpretations:

One: that their plot led them astray until they perished.

The second: that their destruction led their plot astray until it was nullified.

﴿And He sent upon them birds in flocks (ababil)﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. One: that they were from the birds of the sky. This is said by Said ibn Jubayr: "Its like was not seen before or after." Juwaybir narrates from al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: 'It is a bird between the sky and the earth which builds nests and hatches.'" The second opinion: that they were the anqa' al-maghrib, by which proverbs are coined, said by Ikrimah.

The third: that they were from the birds of the earth, which God sent from the direction of the sea, with each bird three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak. This is said by al-Kalbi. They were black, green-beaked, long-necked. It is also said they were like bats (wataawit), and Aisha said they were like swallows (khatatif).

Scholars differed about "ababil" in five opinions. One: that it means many, said by al-Hasan and Tawus.

The second: successive ones following one another, said by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

The third: scattered from here and there, said by Ibn Masud and al-Akhfash, and from it is the poet's saying:

"Indeed Salul, may death overtake you, is a gratitude,
were it not for Salul, we would have walked ababil,"

meaning: scattered.

The fourth: that ababil means of differing colours, said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The fifth: that it means a group after a group, said by Abu Salih and Ata, and from it is the poet's saying:

"And ababil of horses upon them,
like lions of al-Ada beneath the spears."

Ishaq ibn Abdullah ibn al-Harith said: ababil is derived from the camels muʾabbala, which are the herds (aqatii').

The grammarians differed as to whether ababil has a singular of its own kind. Abu Ubayda, al-Farra' and Tha'lab held that it has no singular, like al-abadid and al-samatit. Others held that it has a singular, and they differed about it: Abu Jafar al-Ruwwasi held that its singular is ibbala (with shadda); al-Kisai said its singular is ibwal; and Ibn Kaysan said its singular is ibbil.

﴿Striking them with stones of sijjil﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions. One: that sijjil is a Persian word, sang and gil, the first part being stone and the last part clay, said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that sijjil means hard, said by Abu Ubayda, and from it is Ibn Muqbil's saying:

"And a host striking the helmets from the side,
a striking which the heroes enjoined upon one another, sijjil."

The third: that Sijjil is the name of the lowest heaven, and the stones were attributed to it because they descended from it, said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: that it is the name of a sea of air, from which the stones came, and so they were attributed to it, said by Ikrimah. Concerning the size of the stone there are two opinions:

One: that it was like pebbles for slinging, said by Muqatil.

The second: the stone was larger than a lentil and smaller than a chickpea, said by Abu Salih: "I saw in the house of Umm Hani about a qafiz of the stones with which the companions of the elephant were struck, streaked with red as if they were onyx." Ibn Masud said: "When the birds threw the stones, God sent their wind, which increased them in force, and they did not fall upon anyone without his perishing, and none of them was spared except a man of Kindah," who said:

"Indeed, if you had seen, and you did not see it,
beside the side of al-Mughammas what we met,
I feared God, when He spread birds,
and the shade of a cloud passed over us,
and all of them stayed calling with truth,
as if they had a debt upon the Habshan."

﴿So He made them like eaten stalks﴾. Concerning this there are five opinions:

One: that al-asf is the leaves of the crop, and al-ma'kul is that which the worms have eaten, said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that al-asf al-ma'kul is food, the view of Husayn ibn Thabit.

The third: that it is the husk of wheat after its contents have been eaten, related by Ata ibn al-Sa'ib.

The fourth: that it is the leaves of herbage when the beasts have eaten them and passed them as dung, said by Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: that al-asf is the fig and al-ma'kul is fodder for animals, said by Said ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan.

They differed about what God did to them. Some said that this was a miracle for a prophet who was in that time, and it is said he was Khalid ibn Sinan.

Others said: rather, it was a preparation and consolidation for the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, because he was born in its year, and it is said in its very day.
